analysis.one_liner: Makes corporate mergers that crush competition for workers' wages illegal under antitrust law.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in committee from April 2018 until Congress ended in January 2019, with no markup or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend a 100-year-old antitrust law to say that when one company buys another and gains power over who workers can sell their labor to, that's illegal. Today the law bans mergers that create monopolies (one dominant seller), but says nothing about monopsonies (one dominant buyer) — the situation where a handful of employers control a local labor market and can hold down wages. The bill would also require a government study of how concentration in labor markets affects pay, benefits, and workers' ability to switch jobs.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in labor markets dominated by a few large employers — for example, hospital systems, meatpacking towns, or rural markets where one or two chains employ most workers — would gain a legal tool to challenge mergers that push wages down. The bill's own findings argue that concentrated labor markets let employers dictate wages and restrict worker mobility.

how_it_helps.text: Amends Section 7 of the Clayton Act so that an acquisition tending to create a monopsony — a single buyer with substantial control over a market, including a labor market — violates antitrust law, not just acquisitions tending to create a monopoly.

Requires the Comptroller General to publish, within two years of enactment, a study with public comment on how rising labor-market concentration affects wages and benefits, worker mobility, income equality, and both employees and independent contractors.
States in its findings that in concentrated labor markets employers with monopsony power can dictate wages and use anticompetitive contracts that restrict workers' opportunity and mobility.

analysis.who_pays: Large employers in concentrated labor markets and companies pursuing acquisitions that would consolidate hiring power would face new antitrust exposure — blocked deals and litigation risk. The general public would bear minimal direct cost; enforcement costs would fall on antitrust agencies.

drawbacks.text: The bill is a narrow statutory clarification: inserting two words into the Clayton Act does not by itself guarantee enforcement, and antitrust agencies and courts would still decide case-by-case which mergers 'tend to create' a monopsony, so its practical effect is uncertain.

Mergers that would face new challenges might include some where consolidation brings real efficiencies; blocking acquisitions imposes costs on merging firms and could chill some deals that benefit consumers even as it protects workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The change is small in drafting terms but meaningful in legal terms: it closes a gap where the law polices one dominant seller but not one dominant buyer of labor, which is the situation most likely to hold wages down for ordinary workers. The cost falls on large employers and acquirers, not consumers directly, though over-broad enforcement could block some efficient mergers. On balance the benefit to workers outweighs a modest, manageable cost to businesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, then sent to a Judiciary subcommittee, and died there when Congress ended in January 2019 — no committee vote, no floor vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the bill on April 26, 2018, joined by Reps. Nadler, Ellison, and Crowley.
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee on the day of introduction.
On May 22, 2018, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law — the last action ever taken on it.
The bill had three cosponsors, all Democrats, and never advanced to a markup or floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers in concentrated labor markets are better off: the Clayton Act still says nothing about monopsony power in hiring markets, and consolidating acquisitions face no new antitrust test on the buyer side of labor markets.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so there is no roll-call record; all four original sponsors and all three cosponsors were Democrats, and the committee that buried it was under Republican control.

industries.industry: Large employers in concentrated labor markets
industries.note: The bill would make it harder for dominant employers to hold wages down by blocking acquisitions that concentrate hiring power. Their interest in stopping it runs directly against the workers whose wages it protects.
Acquisitions tending to create a monopsony — including in labor markets — would face new antitrust challenges and litigation risk, raising the cost of consolidation deals.
A new monopsony standard would create work for competition lawyers on both sides of merger challenges. Workers would benefit only if enforcement follows.
